erithacus-rubecula: Both sexes sing, and the autumn song you hear from September is the female claiming a winter territory of her own. Robins hold a patch all year and will fight over it to the death.
troglodytes-troglodytes: One of Britain's smallest birds but one of its loudest: the song is ten times too loud for the size of the bird. In hard winters dozens will roost together in a single nest box for warmth.
regulus-regulus: Britain's smallest bird, weighing about the same as a twenty-pence piece. Its thin, high song sits above 6 kHz, right at the edge of what many adults can hear.
aegithalos-caudatus: Travels in chattering family flocks and huddles in a row along a branch on winter nights. The nest is a stretchy ball of moss, lichen and spider silk lined with up to two thousand feathers.
turdus-merula: The male sings from a high perch at dawn and dusk, one of the finest songs in the garden. Blackbirds fatten up on windfall apples and hedgerow berries through the autumn.
columba-palumbus: The five-note coo, 'take two cows, Taffy', carries across the valley all year. Woodpigeons feed their young on crop milk, a secretion produced by both parents.
cyanistes-caeruleus: A pair can raise a brood of ten or more, timed to the spring peak of caterpillars on oak. The blue crown glows in ultraviolet light, which Blue Tits can see and we can't.
parus-major: The 'teacher, teacher' song is one of the first signs of spring. Great Tits have one of the largest song repertoires of any tit, and each male has several tunes.
coloeus-monedula: Pairs for life and roosts communally, often in church towers and chimneys. The pale eye and the sharp 'jack' call give it away in a flock of rooks.
phasianus-colchicus: Introduced from Asia for shooting, but long naturalised. The male's explosive crow, followed by a whirr of wings, is often the loudest thing on the mic at dawn.
prunella-modularis: Mouse-like and easily overlooked, shuffling under hedges. Its breeding life is anything but dull: females often pair with two males at once.
sitta-europaea: The only British bird that can walk head-first down a tree trunk. Nuthatches plaster mud around the entrance of their nest hole to shrink it to size.
certhia-familiaris: Creeps up a trunk in a spiral like a small mouse, then flies down to the base of the next tree. Its thin call is one of the highest-pitched in the wood.
carduelis-carduelis: The collective noun is a charm, for the tinkling flight calls of a flock. Goldfinches feed on thistle and teasel seed and have become common garden visitors on nyjer.
fringilla-coelebs: One of Britain's commonest breeding birds. The cheerful descending song ends in a flourish, and males learn it from their neighbours, so regional dialects exist.
chloris-chloris: The wheezing 'dzweee' call sounds like a bored teenager. Greenfinch numbers crashed from a parasite spread at bird feeders, so clean feeders matter.
passer-domesticus: Lives alongside people almost everywhere on Earth, yet has declined sharply in Britain since the 1970s. Nests in colonies under roof tiles and in creeper.
sturnus-vulgaris: A gifted mimic that weaves car alarms and curlews into its own song. Winter roosts of tens of thousands form the murmurations seen over reedbeds and piers.
pica-pica: One of the most intelligent birds known; magpies recognise themselves in a mirror. The nest is a domed fortress of sticks with a side entrance.
garrulus-glandarius: The screeching guardian of the wood, more often heard than seen. Jays bury thousands of acorns each autumn and forget enough of them to plant new oaks.
corvus-corone: Usually seen in pairs or small groups, unlike the sociable Rook. Crows have been filmed using tools and dropping shellfish on roads for cars to crack.
corvus-frugilegus: The bare grey face and baggy 'trousers' set it apart from a crow. Rooks nest in noisy colonies at the tops of tall trees and return to the same rookery for generations.
dendrocopos-major: The drumming in late winter is not a call but a signal, hammered against a resonant branch at up to forty beats a second. It has spread into most gardens with feeders.
picus-viridis: The laughing 'yaffle' carries a long way. Green Woodpeckers spend more time on the ground than in trees, digging for ants with a tongue longer than their head.
strix-aluco: The 'tu-whit, tu-whoo' of the nursery rhyme is a duet: the female's 'kewick' answered by the male's hoot. Tawny Owls are strictly nocturnal and never leave their patch.
tyto-alba: Hunts by ear over rough grass at dusk, its face a dish that funnels sound to lopsided ears. The call is a drawn-out shriek, nothing like a hoot.
athene-noctua: Introduced to England in the nineteenth century and now a bird of old orchards, pollards and barns. Often out by day, bobbing on a fence post and glaring.
buteo-buteo: The mewing call overhead is now common across Suffolk after a long recovery. Buzzards soar on broad, fingered wings and will happily walk about a field for worms.
accipiter-nisus: A short-winged, long-tailed hawk built for ambush through hedges and around bird tables. The tiny male catches tits; the much larger female takes pigeons.
falco-tinnunculus: The hovering falcon of road verges, holding its head perfectly still in a wind. Kestrels can see ultraviolet, which lights up the urine trails of voles.
ardea-cinerea: Stands motionless at the water's edge for an hour, then strikes. Herons nest in treetop colonies from February, and their croak in flight sounds prehistoric.
egretta-garzetta: Unknown in Britain thirty years ago, now breeding along the Waveney. The yellow feet on black legs flash as it stirs the shallows for fish.
ardea-alba: Heron-sized and pure white, a recent arrival that now winters and breeds in East Anglia. Watch for the long neck kinked in an S and the slow, deep wingbeats.
alcedo-atthis: A shrill whistle and an electric-blue streak low over the river is usually all you get. Kingfishers nest in a tunnel dug into the bank, and the young fledge smelling of fish.
botaurus-stellaris: Once nearly lost from Britain, the booming of the Bittern is back in East Anglian reedbeds. The foghorn note carries three miles on a still spring night.
circus-aeruginosus: Down to a single pair in 1971, now common over the Broads and marshes. Watch for the V-shaped wings as it quarters low over the reeds.
rallus-aquaticus: Far more often heard than seen: the call is a series of squeals like a piglet being chased. It threads through reedbeds on long toes and is almost never in the open.
cettia-cetti: An explosive burst of song from deep in a bramble, then silence. Cetti's Warbler only colonised Britain in the 1970s and now sings along most East Anglian rivers.
phylloscopus-collybita: Named for its song, a simple 'chiff chaff chiff chaff' that opens the spring. Increasing numbers now stay through the winter rather than migrating to Africa.
phylloscopus-trochilus: Almost identical to a Chiffchaff to look at, but the song is a sweet cascade that falls away at the end. It winters south of the Sahara.
sylvia-atricapilla: A rich, fluting song from spring scrub. Blackcaps from central Europe now winter in British gardens, drawn by feeders, while ours go to Spain.
curruca-communis: A scratchy song delivered in a short bouncing display flight over a hedge. Whitethroats arrive from the Sahel in April and go back in September.
hirundo-rustica: Nests on a beam in barns and porches, returning to the same building each spring from South Africa. A swallow feeding chicks catches up to 6,000 insects a day.
delichon-urbicum: Builds a mud cup under the eaves and lines the underside of roofs with a row of nests. Numbers have fallen steeply, so a colony is worth protecting.
apus-apus: Eats, sleeps and mates on the wing, landing only to nest. Swifts arrive in early May and are gone again by early August, screaming round the rooftops in between.
cuculus-canorus: The two-note call says spring, but the bird is a brood parasite that leaves its eggs in Dunnock and Reed Warbler nests. Adults leave for Africa by July.
motacilla-alba: The bobbing black-and-white bird of car parks and rooftops. Pied Wagtails gather in winter roosts in town-centre trees, hundreds strong under the street lights.
motacilla-cinerea: Despite the name, the yellow belly is what you notice. Grey Wagtails nest by fast water, mill races and weirs, and flick their long tails constantly.
anthus-pratensis: A small streaky pipit of rough grass, with a thin 'sip sip' call. It is the commonest host of the Cuckoo on moorland and the staple prey of the Merlin.
anthus-trivialis: A summer visitor to woodland edges, best told by its parachuting song flight. In September one may pass through the garden on migration, calling a buzzy 'teez'.
emberiza-citrinella: 'A little bit of bread and no cheese' is the classic rendering of the song from a hedge-top. The bright yellow head of a spring male is unmistakable.
emberiza-schoeniclus: A sparrow-like bunting of reedbeds and wet ditches; the male has a black hood and white collar. It has spread into oilseed rape fields and garden feeders in winter.
linaria-cannabina: Twittering flocks over stubble in winter, and a male with a pink breast in spring. Linnets feed almost entirely on seeds, even feeding seeds to their young.
spinus-spinus: A small streaky finch of alder and birch, appearing in gardens in late winter when wild seed runs out. Flocks hang upside down from the cones.
pyrrhula-pyrrhula: The soft piped call and a flash of white rump are often all you get of this shy finch. The rose-pink male is a striking sight on a bare hedge.
coccothraustes-coccothraustes: The bird with a bill that can crack a cherry stone. Hawfinches are rare and elusive in Suffolk, feeding high in hornbeams, and any record is a good one.
turdus-philomelos: Sings each phrase two or three times over, which is how to tell it from a Blackbird. Song Thrushes smash snails on a favourite 'anvil' stone.
turdus-viscivorus: The 'stormcock', singing from the top of a tall tree in wild weather. Its rattling alarm call is like a football rattle, and it defends berry-laden trees all winter.
turdus-pilaris: A winter thrush from Scandinavia, arriving in October in chuckling flocks with Redwings. The first Fieldfare of the autumn is a real marker of the season turning.
turdus-iliacus: Listen on still October nights for the thin 'seep' calls overhead: Redwings migrating from Iceland and Scandinavia. The red flank and pale eyebrow separate it from a Song Thrush.
streptopelia-decaocto: Spread across Europe from the Balkans in a few decades and first bred in Britain in 1955. The three-note coo is often mistaken for a Cuckoo by the hopeful.
columba-oenas: A neater, greyer pigeon than the Woodpigeon, with no white on the neck. Stock Doves nest in holes in old trees and give a deep, two-note grunt of a song.
anas-platyrhynchos: The familiar duck of every pond, and the ancestor of most farmyard ducks. Only the female quacks; the drake's call is a quiet rasp.
gallinula-chloropus: The red-and-yellow bill and constantly flicking white undertail make it easy. Moorhens are surprisingly aggressive and will fight with their feet.
fulica-atra: 'Bald as a coot' refers to the white shield above the bill. Coots are quarrelsome and noisy, with a sharp 'kowk' that carries across any lake.
cygnus-olor: Britain's heaviest flying bird, with a wingbeat you can hear from across the water. The throbbing hum of the wings in flight is the sound that gives it the name.
branta-canadensis: Introduced in the seventeenth century as an ornamental bird and now everywhere. The honking V-formations overhead are one of the sounds of autumn.
anser-anser: The wild ancestor of the farmyard goose. Greylags gabble in flight and are now resident on most Suffolk gravel pits and marshes.
vanellus-vanellus: The 'peewit', named for its call, with a tumbling display flight over spring fields. Once abundant on farmland, now a bird to celebrate when it appears.
numenius-arquata: The bubbling call of the Curlew is the sound of estuaries and wild places. Europe's largest wader, with a bill that can probe deep mud for worms.
haematopus-ostralegus: A loud, piping black-and-white wader with a carrot bill. Oystercatchers rarely eat oysters; mussels, cockles and worms are the real diet.
larus-argentatus: The archetypal seagull, though many now nest on rooftops far inland. The long, laughing call is one of the sounds of the British coast.
chroicocephalus-ridibundus: The commonest gull inland, following the plough in winter. The chocolate hood is worn only in the breeding season and fades to a dark ear-spot.
phalacrocorax-carbo: Increasingly seen inland on rivers and lakes, standing with wings spread to dry. A cormorant can dive to thirty metres and eat a pound of fish a day.
tachybaptus-ruficollis: A tiny, dumpy grebe that dives at the first sign of trouble and pops up somewhere else. The whinnying trill from a reedy pond is the giveaway.
podiceps-cristatus: Nearly hunted out of Britain for its head plumes in the 1860s, which helped start the RSPB. The spring courtship 'weed dance' is one of nature's great displays.
regulus-ignicapilla: A Goldcrest with a black eyestripe and a white eyebrow, and a bronze shoulder patch. Once a rarity, Firecrests now breed in Suffolk and pass through in autumn.
phoenicurus-ochruros: A bird of quarries, power stations and bombed cities, and a scarce passage migrant in Suffolk. The rusty, shivering tail is diagnostic. Treat a single detection with caution.
phoenicurus-phoenicurus: A summer visitor to old oak woodland in the west; in Suffolk it is mostly seen on passage in spring and autumn. The flame-orange tail quivers constantly.
muscicapa-striata: A summer visitor that sits upright on a bare twig and sallies out after flies. Spotted Flycatchers have declined by nearly ninety percent since the 1960s.
poecile-palustris: A small brown tit with a glossy black cap and a sneezing 'pitchoo' call. It caches seeds in bark crevices and remembers where it put them.
periparus-ater: The smallest British tit, with a white stripe down the back of its black head. Coal Tits prefer conifers and hoard seeds from feeders through the autumn.
lophophanes-cristatus: A tit of Scottish pinewoods, with a pointed black-and-white crest. Very rare in England, so any detection here is almost certainly a mistake.
streptopelia-turtur: The purring song of the Turtle Dove was once the sound of an English summer; the bird has declined by 98 percent. Any record on the mic is precious.
perdix-perdix: The native Grey Partridge, once common on every farm and now scarce. The creaky 'kirr-ic' call at dusk is the way to find them.
alectoris-rufa: Introduced from France for shooting, with a red bill and bold flank bars. Red-legged Partridges prefer to run rather than fly and call a rhythmic 'chuck-chuck-or'.
dryobates-minor: Sparrow-sized and rarely seen, the Lesser Spotted Woodpecker is one of Britain's fastest-declining birds. Listen for a high 'pee-pee-pee' call in early spring.
scolopax-rusticola: A woodland wader with eyes set to see all round. At dusk in spring the male 'rodes' over the wood with a croak and a squeak. Winter arrivals come from Russia.
caprimulgus-europaeus: The Nightjar churrs at dusk on heaths, a mechanical purr that can last for minutes. Suffolk's Sandlings hold a good population from May to August.
corvus-corax: The largest crow, with a deep croak and a wedge-shaped tail. Ravens have returned to East Anglia after two centuries of absence and now breed in Suffolk.
falco-peregrinus: The fastest animal on Earth in its hunting stoop, at over 200 mph. Peregrines now nest on cathedrals, cooling towers and pylons across Suffolk.
pandion-haliaetus: A fish-eating hawk that passes through Suffolk on migration in spring and autumn. Watch for it hovering over the river then plunging feet-first.
bubulcus-ibis: A small egret that follows cattle and horses for the insects they kick up. Once a great rarity, it now breeds in Britain and turns up in Waveney Valley pastures.
grus-grus: Cranes bred in the Norfolk Broads for the first time in four hundred years in 1981 and are slowly spreading. The bugling call carries for miles.
anas-crecca: The smallest British duck, whistling softly on a winter marsh. Flocks spring vertically from the water when alarmed, which is where 'spring' for a group of teal comes from.
asio-flammeus: A day-flying owl of rough grassland and marsh, wintering in East Anglia from the north. It quarters low like a harrier with slow, stiff wingbeats.
asio-otus: The most secretive British owl, roosting by day in dense thorn or ivy. The song is a low, moaning hoot, easily missed under a Tawny Owl.
milvus-milvus: Reintroduced in the 1990s and now spreading east across Suffolk. The forked tail and the mewing whistle are the marks of a Red Kite overhead.
sterna-hirundo: The 'sea swallow', returning from West Africa in April to nest on shingle and rafts. The harsh 'kee-yah' call carries over water.
riparia-riparia: The smallest and earliest of the swallows, back in March to nest in tunnels in sandy river banks and quarry faces. Colonies can number hundreds of holes.
corvus-monedula: Pairs for life and roosts communally, often in church towers and chimneys. The pale eye and the sharp 'jack' call give it away in a flock of rooks.
sylvia-communis: A scratchy song delivered in a short bouncing display flight over a hedge. Whitethroats arrive from the Sahel in April and go back in September.
carduelis-cannabina: Twittering flocks over stubble in winter, and a male with a pink breast in spring. Linnets feed almost entirely on seeds, even feeding seeds to their young.
carduelis-spinus: A small streaky finch of alder and birch, appearing in gardens in late winter when wild seed runs out. Flocks hang upside down from the cones.
carduelis-chloris: The wheezing 'dzweee' call sounds like a bored teenager. Greenfinch numbers crashed from a parasite spread at bird feeders, so clean feeders matter.
dendrocopos-minor: Sparrow-sized and rarely seen, the Lesser Spotted Woodpecker is one of Britain's fastest-declining birds. Listen for a high 'pee-pee-pee' call in early spring.
regulus-ignicapillus: A Goldcrest with a black eyestripe and a white eyebrow, and a bronze shoulder patch. Once a rarity, Firecrests now breed in Suffolk and pass through in autumn.
acanthis-cabaret: A small streaky finch with a red forehead, feeding acrobatically on birch and alder seed in winter. Flocks give a hard metallic 'chett-chett' in flight.
accipiter-gentilis: A Sparrowhawk scaled up to Buzzard size, and a bird of big forests that has crept back into East Anglia from Thetford. Its display flight over the trees in early spring is the best chance of seeing one.
acrocephalus-schoenobaenus: A summer visitor to reedy ditches with a bold cream eyebrow and a fast, scratchy, restless song. Sedge Warblers never repeat a phrase the same way twice.
acrocephalus-scirpaceus: Plain brown and hard to see in the reeds, but the rhythmic churring song gives it away all summer. The Cuckoo's favourite host in East Anglia.
actitis-hypoleucos: A small wader that bobs constantly and flies low over the water with stiff, flickering wingbeats. It passes along rivers and lake edges in spring and late summer.
alauda-arvensis: The song of open farmland, delivered in a hovering flight so high the bird is a speck. Skylarks have declined by more than half since the 1970s as farming changed.
alca-torda: A black-and-white seabird of cliffs and open sea, with a deep bill marked by a white line. Only a stray would be heard this far inland, so treat a record with suspicion.
alopochen-aegyptiaca: Introduced from Africa as an ornamental bird and now common on Norfolk and Suffolk waters. It nests early, often in a hollow tree, and is loud and quarrelsome.
anas-acuta: The most elegant of the dabbling ducks, long-necked with a needle tail on the drake. A winter visitor to marshes and estuaries, rarely far inland.
anser-albifrons: Winter geese from Russia with a white face patch and black belly bars, feeding on grazing marsh. The high, laughing calls carry across the flats.
anser-brachyrhynchus: Norfolk hosts a large part of the world's Pink-footed Geese each winter, and skeins pass over Suffolk at dawn and dusk. The call is a high 'wink-wink'.
anthus-petrosus: A dark pipit of rocky shores and sea walls, unlikely inland. It walks among seaweed and rocks picking insects and small snails.
arenaria-interpres: A stocky wader that flips seaweed and stones to find food, as its name says. A bird of the coast; a valley record would be unusual.
aythya-ferina: A diving duck with a chestnut head and a grey back, wintering on gravel pits and lakes. Numbers have fallen sharply across Europe.
aythya-fuligula: The commonest diving duck on ponds and lakes, the drake black and white with a drooping crest. Dives for snails and insect larvae.
branta-bernicla: A small dark goose that winters on the Suffolk estuaries after breeding in Siberia, feeding on eelgrass on the mud. A soft, rolling 'rronk' in flocks.
branta-leucopsis: A black-and-white goose with a cream face. Wild birds winter on the Solway; those in East Anglia are mostly from feral flocks.
bucephala-clangula: A winter diving duck with a bold white cheek spot on the drake. The wings whistle in flight, which is how the name came about.
calidris-alba: A pale wader that runs along the tide edge like clockwork, chasing waves. Strictly coastal; it breeds in the high Arctic.
calidris-alpina: The commonest small wader on British estuaries, in flocks that twist and flash over the mud. Rarely far from the coast.
calidris-canutus: Knot winter on the Wash in flocks of tens of thousands, one of Britain's great wildlife spectacles. Unlikely inland.
calidris-ferruginea: A passage wader from Siberia with a down-curved bill, seen on the coast in late summer. An inland record would be a good one.
calidris-minuta: A tiny wader of autumn passage on the coast, smaller than a sparrow. Little Stints feed with quick, nervous pecks along the shore.
calidris-pugnax: Once bred widely in the Fens; now mostly a passage bird and winter visitor to wet meadows. The name refers to the males' extraordinary breeding plumage.
certhia-brachydactyla: A continental species almost identical to our Treecreeper, and a rarity in Britain. A record here is far more likely to be a Treecreeper.
charadrius-dubius: A small plover of gravel pits and quarry floors, with a yellow eye-ring. A summer visitor that only colonised Britain in the 1940s.
charadrius-hiaticula: A plover of sandy and shingle beaches with a black breast band and orange bill. Its soft, rising 'too-lee' call is heard on most coasts.
cinclus-cinclus: A bird of fast upland rivers that walks under water to feed. There are no Dippers in Suffolk, so treat a detection as a mistake.
circus-cyaneus: A grey male or brown 'ringtail' female quartering low over marsh in winter. Hen Harriers roost communally on the coast; inland sightings are scarce.
cisticola-juncidis: A tiny Mediterranean warbler with a bouncing song flight, slowly spreading north. A great rarity in Britain; a detection here is almost certainly wrong.
columba-livia: The town pigeon, descended from the wild Rock Dove of sea cliffs. Feral birds come in every colour; the wild form has two black wingbars and a white rump.
corvus-cornix: The grey-bodied crow of Scotland, Ireland and the continent. In Suffolk it is a scarce winter visitor from Scandinavia, and easily confused with a Carrion Crow.
curruca-curruca: A neat grey-and-white warbler with a dark mask, whose song is a dry rattle after a quiet warble. A summer visitor to hedges and scrub.
cygnus-cygnus: A wild swan from Iceland, wintering in East Anglia in smaller numbers than the Bewick's. The yellow bill and bugling calls set it apart from the Mute Swan.
emberiza-cirlus: A bunting of Devon hedgerows, long lost from East Anglia. Any record here is a misidentified Yellowhammer.
falco-columbarius: Britain's smallest falcon, wintering on marshes and coasts from the uplands. It hunts small birds in a low, dashing chase.
falco-subbuteo: A summer falcon that catches dragonflies and swallows on the wing, shaped like a giant swift. Hobbies breed in old crows' nests across Suffolk.
ficedula-hypoleuca: A summer visitor to western oak woods, seen in the east only on migration. A black-and-white male in spring is a striking bird.
fringilla-montifringilla: The northern cousin of the Chaffinch, arriving from Scandinavia in autumn. Bramblings love beech mast and join Chaffinch flocks in winter.
fulmarus-glacialis: A gull-like seabird that is really a petrel, gliding on stiff wings along cliffs. It nests on the Suffolk cliffs at Hunstanton and would not be heard inland.
gallinago-gallinago: A long-billed wader of wet grassland that zigzags away when flushed. In spring the male 'drums', diving with stiff tail feathers that hum in the air.
gavia-stellata: Divers winter off the Suffolk coast in good numbers, but stay at sea. A detection inland is a mistake.
haliaeetus-albicilla: Britain's largest bird of prey, with a two-metre wingspan. Young birds from the Isle of Wight reintroduction now wander across East Anglia.
himantopus-himantopus: An elegant black-and-white wader on absurdly long pink legs. A rare visitor from the south that has bred in Britain a handful of times.
hydrocoloeus-minutus: The world's smallest gull, seen on passage over coastal waters and occasionally on inland lakes. Dainty and tern-like in flight.
ichthyaetus-melanocephalus: A gull with a jet-black hood and pure white wingtips, spreading rapidly in Britain. The call is a distinctive 'yeow'.
larus-cachinnans: A large gull from the east, increasingly found at rubbish tips and reservoirs in winter. Hard to separate from a Herring Gull.
larus-canus: A gentle-looking gull with a yellow-green bill, common on fields inland in winter. Its name has nothing to do with being common.
larus-fuscus: A dark-backed gull with yellow legs, now breeding on rooftops and rubbish tips far inland. Many still migrate to Iberia for winter.
larus-marinus: The largest gull in the world, with a black back and a heavy bill. A predator of other birds' chicks on the coast.
larus-michahellis: A Mediterranean gull that has spread north; scarce but regular in Suffolk, especially in late summer. Yellow legs and a darker back than a Herring Gull.
limosa-lapponica: A wader of the estuaries, wintering on the Wash and Suffolk coast. One tracked bird flew from Alaska to New Zealand in nine days without stopping.
limosa-limosa: A tall wader with a long straight bill, breeding in wet meadows on the Ouse Washes and wintering on estuaries. Rusty-red in spring.
loxia-curvirostra: A finch with crossed mandibles for prising seeds from pine cones. Flocks visit the Brecks and the Sandlings, calling 'chip chip' overhead.
luscinia-svecica: A scarce migrant with a brilliant blue throat, mostly seen on the coast in spring and autumn. A record inland would be exceptional.
mareca-penelope: A winter duck in whistling flocks, grazing on marsh grass like geese. The drake has a chestnut head with a cream forehead.
mareca-strepera: A subtle grey dabbling duck with a white wing patch, now breeding widely on East Anglian waters. Often steals food from diving Coots.
melanitta-nigra: A sea duck wintering in rafts off the Suffolk coast. All black, and only heard from the shore on calm nights.
mergus-merganser: A fish-eating diving duck with a serrated bill, wintering on gravel pits and rivers. The drake is white with a bottle-green head.
mergus-serrator: A sea-going sawbill with a shaggy crest, wintering in estuaries and along the coast. Rarely far inland.
morus-bassanus: Britain's largest seabird, diving into the sea from thirty metres. Gannets pass along the Suffolk coast in autumn; a detection inland is a mistake.
motacilla-flava: A summer visitor to wet meadows and crop fields, the male bright yellow below. Declining, and now scarce in Suffolk.
numenius-phaeopus: A smaller, striped-headed relative of the Curlew, passing through in spring and autumn. Its seven-note whistle can be heard overhead at night on migration.
oenanthe-oenanthe: A bird of open ground with a white rump, passing through on migration to and from Africa. Often seen on ploughed fields in spring.
panurus-biarmicus: A reedbed specialist with a long tail, the male with black moustaches. Listen for pinging calls from the reeds at Minsmere and along the Waveney.
passer-montanus: A neater sparrow with a chestnut cap and a black cheek spot, now scarce after a huge decline. Nests in holes in old trees and farm buildings.
pernis-apivorus: A rare summer visitor that raids wasp nests for grubs. A handful breed in Britain, and one passing over Suffolk in September is plausible on migration, but a single detection deserves caution.
phylloscopus-inornatus: A tiny Siberian warbler that reaches the east coast every autumn in small numbers. Listen for its loud, rising 'tsweest' in coastal scrub in October.
platalea-leucorodia: A large white heron-like bird with a spoon-shaped bill, back breeding in Norfolk after centuries away. Feeds by sweeping the bill through shallow water.
pluvialis-apricaria: Golden Plovers winter in large flocks on ploughed fields and marshes, often with Lapwings. The mournful whistle is a sound of winter fields.
pluvialis-squatarola: A wader of the estuary mud, silver-grey in winter with black armpits in flight. Strictly coastal.
podiceps-auritus: A rare grebe that winters in small numbers off the coast and on a few reservoirs. Unlikely to be heard here.
podiceps-nigricollis: A small grebe with a golden ear tuft in summer, breeding at a few East Anglian sites. Dives constantly and is rarely seen in flight.
psittacula-krameri: The bright green parakeet of London parks, spreading slowly outwards. Still scarce in Suffolk, but the screeching call is unmistakable.
puffinus-puffinus: A seabird that spends its life at sea and comes ashore only to nest in burrows on western islands. A detection inland is a mistake.
pyrrhocorax-pyrrhocorax: A red-billed crow of western sea cliffs, absent from East Anglia. Any record here is wrong.
recurvirostra-avosetta: The emblem of the RSPB, which returned to breed at Minsmere in 1947 after a century away. It sweeps its upturned bill through shallow water.
rissa-tridactyla: A gentle-looking cliff-nesting gull that spends winter far out at sea. Kittiwakes nest on the pier at Lowestoft, but would not be heard inland.
saxicola-rubetra: A summer visitor to rough grassland with a bold pale eyebrow, seen in Suffolk mainly on migration. Perches on tall stems and fence posts.
saxicola-rubicola: A small chat that sits on top of gorse and bramble, the male with a black head and orange breast. The call sounds like two pebbles being knocked together.
somateria-mollissima: A heavy sea duck of northern coasts, with the drake's crooning 'ah-ooo' call. Small numbers winter off Suffolk; not a valley bird.
spatula-clypeata: A dabbling duck with an enormous shovel of a bill, sifting the water for plankton. Winters on marshes across East Anglia.
spatula-querquedula: A summer duck, the drake with a white crescent over the eye. A scarce breeder in East Anglian marshes; its call is a dry rattle.
stercorarius-parasiticus: A pirate of the sea that chases terns until they drop their fish. Passes along the coast in autumn; not an inland bird.
sternula-albifrons: Britain's smallest tern, nesting on shingle beaches on the Suffolk coast. Its colonies are fenced against foxes and feet.
sylvia-borin: A plain brown warbler with a rich, even song, easily confused with a Blackcap's. A summer visitor to scrub and woodland edge.
tadorna-tadorna: A large, goose-like duck of estuaries, boldly patterned in white, chestnut and green. Shelducks nest in old rabbit burrows.
thalasseus-sandvicensis: A big, pale tern with a shaggy crest and a harsh 'kirrik' call, breeding in colonies on the coast. Passes overhead on migration.
tringa-erythropus: A passage wader from the Arctic, jet black in breeding plumage. Best known from coastal lagoons in autumn.
tringa-glareola: A slim wader of freshwater margins, seen on passage in spring and autumn. Its call is a sharp 'chiff-iff-iff'.
tringa-nebularia: A tall, grey wader with a slightly upturned bill and a ringing three-note call. Passes through on the way to and from Scotland.
tringa-ochropus: A dark wader with a white rump that flushes from ditches with a loud, liquid call. Winters in small numbers on Suffolk streams.
tringa-totanus: The 'sentinel of the marshes', with red legs and a nervous, yelping alarm. Breeds on wet grassland and winters on the estuaries.
turdus-torquatus: The mountain Blackbird, with a white crescent on the breast. Passes through the east on migration in spring and autumn.
uria-aalge: A seabird of cliff ledges, standing upright like a penguin. Only seen in Suffolk on the sea; a detection here is a mistake.
